title: Misuse and fakes
objectives: Recognise common misuses of AI: cheating on assessed work, fake reviews, scams and faked media.

screens.prose: Three reviews of a restaurant. One was written by a chatbot, to order, by someone who never ate there. All three are invented.

rows: Lovely evening. The lamb was tender, the staff were friendly and the bill was fair. We will be back.
Good food but slow. Waited 40 minutes for mains on a quiet Tuesday. Dessert made up for it.
Best pasta in town, though the music was a bit loud. Booking ahead is a must at weekends.

screens.question: Which one was written to order?

options.text: You cannot reliably tell from the text
Review 1, because it is the most polished
options.why: Polish is no sign either way now: a chatbot writes rough or smooth on request.

options.text: Review 2, because its details sound made up
options.why: Specific details are cheap to invent. They do not show who wrote it.

options.text: Review 3, because it mixes praise with a complaint
options.why: A fake can add a small complaint to look real.

hints.text: What would a chatbot asked for "a believable review" write?
Look at how ordinary all three are.
Each could be real or fake. Fluent, ordinary text is now cheap to produce.

feedback.correct: You cannot tell reliably. Here the fake was review 1, but any of them could have been.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the text alone could show who wrote it.

explain.text: In this example the fake was review 1, but nothing in the text gives it away. A chatbot can write rough or smooth, glowing or mixed, on request. Fluent writing no longer tells you who wrote it, or whether they were there.

screens.prose: Fake reviews are one **misuse** of AI. Others: passing off AI work as your own where that is not allowed, fake accounts, scam messages that read well, and faked voices and images.

rows: Lovely evening. The lamb was tender, the staff were friendly and the bill was fair. We will be back.
Good food but slow. Waited 40 minutes for mains on a quiet Tuesday. Dessert made up for it.
Best pasta in town, though the music was a bit loud. Booking ahead is a must at weekends.

screens.question: Select all that apply: which of these are misuses?

options.text: Posting 50 reviews of your own café under made-up names
Handing in a chatbot's essay as your own on marked coursework that forbids it
Making a fake voice note of a real person asking for money
Using a chatbot to tidy a review of a meal you really ate, then posting it as yours
options.why: That is an honest use: the experience is yours, and so is the review. The tool only tidied it.

options.text: Using a clearly labelled AI-made picture on a poster
options.why: Labelled, it deceives no one.

hints.text: In which cases is someone deceived?
Ask who is misled, and about what.
Fake reviewers, a hidden essay and a faked voice all deceive. A real review tidied up, and a labelled picture, do not.

feedback.correct: The three that deceive someone: fake reviews, a hidden essay, a faked voice.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask in each case whether anyone is deceived.

explain.text: A misuse deceives someone: buyers, a teacher, or the person who hears a faked voice. The same tools used openly, on your own work or with a label, deceive no one.

screens.prose: A message arrives. It reads well, and that tells you nothing. Look for the signs instead.

lines: From: Accounts Team <payments@secure-bankk-help.example>
Dear customer, we noticed unusual activity on your account.
You must act within 30 minutes or your account will be closed.
To keep it open, pay a £1 check fee at the link below.
https://secure-bankk-help.example/verify
Thank you for banking with us.
params.title: An invented message

screens.question: Tap every warning sign.

hints.text: Look for hurry, money and odd addresses.
Compare the address with your real bank's.
An odd sender, a 30-minute deadline, a payment request and a link to an odd site are all warning signs.

feedback.correct: The odd sender, the deadline, the payment request and the odd link.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for urgency, a payment request and addresses that do not match.

byKey.l2: Mentioning unusual activity is common in real messages too. On its own it is not a sign.
byKey.l6: A polite sign-off is no sign either way.

explain.text: Urgency stops you thinking, a payment request is the goal, and the address and link do not match a real bank. Fluent wording is now cheap, so these signs matter more than the writing.

screens.prose: Each misuse does a different kind of harm.

lines: From: Accounts Team <payments@secure-bankk-help.example>
Dear customer, we noticed unusual activity on your account.
You must act within 30 minutes or your account will be closed.
To keep it open, pay a £1 check fee at the link below.
https://secure-bankk-help.example/verify
Thank you for banking with us.
params.title: An invented message

screens.question: Drag each misuse to its harm.

tokens.text: A faked voice of a boss
An AI essay passed off as yours
A scam message that reads well

slots.label: Hides what you can really do
Steals money or passwords from the public

hints.text: Who is deceived in each case?
A faked boss's voice is aimed at staff.
Reviews mislead buyers; a faked boss tricks staff; a hidden essay misleads a teacher about you; a scam steals from the public.

feedback.correct: Each misuse matched to who it deceives and how.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask who is deceived in each case.

byKey.reviews: Fake reviews mislead people choosing what to buy.
byKey.voice: A faked boss's voice is aimed at staff who can make payments.
byKey.essay: An essay passed off as yours misleads your teacher about what you can do.
byKey.scam: A well-written scam aims to take money or passwords.

explain.text: Each misuse deceives someone different: buyers, staff, a teacher, the public. Naming the harm tells you who should be careful and what to check.

screens.prose: You get a voice note that sounds exactly like your brother, asking you to send £300 at once to a new account.

lines: Voice note, 0:14: "It's me. My card's blocked. Can you send £300 to this new account right now? I'll explain later."
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: What should you do first?

options.text: Call your brother on the number you already have for him
Reply to the voice note to ask if it is really him
options.why: The faker controls that channel, so they will say yes.

options.text: Send the money, since it is his voice
options.why: A voice can now be faked from a short recording. It proves nothing.

options.text: Listen again closely for signs it is fake
options.why: A good fake may have none. A check through another channel is far stronger.

hints.text: Which channel does the faker not control?
You already have his number.
Call him on the number you know. If it was not him, you have lost nothing.

feedback.correct: Check through a channel you already trust: his known number.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which channel the faker cannot control.

explain.text: A voice can be faked, and the faker controls the message they sent. A channel you already trusted before the message, such as his known number, is outside their reach. Call it before you pay anything.

screens.prose: A colleague says of an email asking for a password reset: "It is perfectly written, with no spelling mistakes, so it must be genuine."

lines: From: Accounts Team <payments@secure-bankk-help.example>
Dear customer, we noticed unusual activity on your account.
You must act within 30 minutes or your account will be closed.
To keep it open, pay a £1 check fee at the link below.
https://secure-bankk-help.example/verify
Thank you for banking with us.
params.title: An invented message

screens.question: Is she right?

options.text: No: fluent writing is now cheap, so it proves nothing
Yes: scams are full of mistakes, and this has none
options.why: You used good spelling as a sign of a real sender. A chatbot writes flawless scams on request.

options.text: Yes, if it is also long
options.why: Length proves nothing either.

options.text: No: every perfectly written email is a scam
options.why: Most real emails are well written too. Writing tells you nothing either way.

hints.text: Who can now write flawless text in seconds?
Look again at the address and the link.
Spelling is no longer a test. The signs are the address, the link, the urgency and the request.

feedback.correct: Good writing no longer separates real from fake. Check the signs and the sender.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what it costs a scammer to write well now.

byKey.fluent: You took flawless spelling as proof of a real sender. Chatbots make fluent text cheap, so scams no longer need mistakes.

explain.text: Spelling mistakes used to give many scams away. A chatbot now writes fluent text for anyone, in seconds. So judge a message by its sender, link, urgency and request, and check through a channel you trust.

screens.prose: The same tools have honest uses. Each case below is invented.

rows: A student uses a chatbot to quiz herself before an exam
A shop posts an AI-made picture labelled "AI image"
A firm posts chatbot-written reviews of itself as "customers"
A writer has a chatbot tidy the grammar of his own review of a real meal

screens.question: Tap the one case that is a misuse.

hints.text: In which case is someone deceived?
Who wrote case R's reviews?
R presents the firm's own writing as customers' views. The others are open or about the person's own work.

feedback.correct: Case R deceives buyers. The others are honest uses.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask in each case whether anyone is deceived.

byKey.r0: Quizzing yourself is an honest use: no one is deceived.
byKey.r1: A labelled AI picture deceives no one.
byKey.r3: His review is of a real meal, in his own words, only tidied.

explain.text: A tool is not a misuse in itself. Quizzing yourself, a labelled picture and a tidied review of a real meal deceive no one. Posing as customers does.

screens.prose: Writing, voices and pictures can all be made to order now: $$\text{fluent} \neq \text{genuine}$$ So judge a message by its sender and its request, and check through a channel you already trust.
screens.question: A text "from your bank" asks you to call a number in the message. What is the safe check?

options.text: Call the number on the back of your bank card instead
Call the number in the text
options.why: The sender controls that number.

options.text: Reply to the text and ask if it is real
options.why: The sender controls that channel too.

options.text: Read the text again for mistakes
options.why: Good wording proves nothing now.

feedback.correct: A number you already trust, such as the one on your card.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which channel the sender does not control.

screens.prose: A desk receives a voice note that sounds exactly like the head of trading: "Urgent. Wire £250,000 to this new account before the close. Do not call me, I am in a meeting." The desk has a call-back rule.

lines: Desk rule 7: before any payment requested by voice, phone or message,
call the requester back on the number in the firm's own directory.
params.title: An invented desk rule

screens.question: What does the call-back rule have the desk do?

options.text: Call the head of trading on her number in the firm's directory before paying
Pay at once, since the voice and the urgency both sound right
options.why: A voice can be faked, and urgency is a warning sign. The rule exists for exactly this.

options.text: Reply to the voice note to confirm it is really her
options.why: The faker controls that channel and will confirm.

options.text: Wait until her meeting is over, then pay
options.why: Waiting is wise, but the payment still needs a call on the directory number.

hints.text: Which number does the rule say to use?
Read the second line.
The directory number is outside the faker's control. "Do not call me" is itself a warning sign.

feedback.correct: Call back on the directory number before any payment. "Do not call me" is a warning sign.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read what the rule says.

explain.text: A faked voice, urgency and "do not call me" are the pattern of this scam. The call-back rule sends the check through a channel the faker cannot control: the firm's own directory. One short call stops the payment.

ideas: Common misuses: passing off AI work as your own where it is not allowed, fake reviews and accounts, scam messages, and faked voices and images.
Fluent writing, a familiar voice or a real-looking picture is now cheap to make, so none of them proves a message is genuine.
Check through a channel you already trust, such as a known number. The same tools used openly, on your own work, deceive no one.

formula.name: Fakes
formula.note: Judge the sender and the request, and check through a channel you trust.

summary.trap: "It is well written, so it must be genuine" is wrong. Fluency is now cheap.

quiz.question: Why are good spelling and grammar no longer a sign that a message is genuine?

options.text: Chatbots let anyone write fluent text in seconds
Everyone now spells perfectly
options.why: People still make mistakes. The change is that fluent text is cheap to make.

options.text: Banks have stopped checking their emails
options.why: Banks still check. Scammers no longer need to make mistakes.

options.text: They never were a sign of anything
options.why: Mistakes once gave many scams away. That sign has gone.

feedback.correct: Fluent text is now cheap for anyone, scammers included.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what changed for the people writing scams.

explain.text: Many scams used to give themselves away with poor writing. A chatbot now produces fluent text for anyone, so writing quality no longer separates real from fake.

quiz.question: A message from a colleague's account asks you to buy gift cards urgently. What is the best check?

options.text: Phone the colleague on a number you already know
Reply to the message to ask if it is them
options.why: If the account is taken over, the faker will reply.

options.text: Check the message for spelling mistakes
options.why: A scammer can write without mistakes.

options.text: Buy one card first, to test
options.why: Any payment is what the scam wants.

feedback.correct: A channel you already trust, outside the faker's reach.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which channel the faker cannot control.

explain.text: If the account is taken over, every reply comes from the faker. A number you already knew is outside their control, so check through it before you buy anything.

quiz.question: Which is an honest use of a chatbot?

options.text: Asking it to quiz you on your own revision notes
Writing reviews of your own shop under customers' names
options.why: That deceives buyers.

options.text: Handing in its essay as your own where that is forbidden
options.why: That deceives the person marking it.

options.text: Copying a friend's voice to prank-call their bank
options.why: Faking a real person's voice to a bank deceives the bank.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the case where no one is deceived.

explain.text: Using a chatbot to quiz yourself is honest: you are the only one involved, and no one is misled. The other uses each deceive someone.
